lead: Sweet Georgia Brown was a skin-lightening cream sold in the United States, with advertising pictured from the 1930s. It belongs to a long history of bleaching creams marketed to even out or lighten the skin.
Its place in the wiki is historical: it illustrates how skin-lightening products were advertised in the Jim Crow era and how those products drew on beauty norms favouring lighter skin.

paras: Such creams were applied to the face and body over time with the goal of lightening skin tone. No modern use is documented.
Historical bleaching products frequently contained hidden mercury or other toxic ingredients, and modern bleaching agents such as hydroquinone and steroids carry documented harms.

angle.text: The product was marketed to lighten the complexion. How much it did so is not documented; this is a historical brand.

lead: Sweet Georgia Brown was a skin-bleaching cream whose 1930s advertisement is reproduced on Wikipedia's skin whitening article [1]. Specific details of its formulation, maker and sales are not documented in the sources consulted.

Wikipedia places such products in a longer American history: lightening recipes brought by European immigrants, ceruse and arsenic wafers in the 1800s, and marketing of bleaching creams to Black women documented from the mid-19th century, which historians link to the Jim Crow era and its messages that lighter skin was "cleaner and better" [1].

paras: Early US skin whiteners were first used mainly by white women, and use among Black American women is documented from the mid-19th century [1]. The 1960s Black is Beautiful movement temporarily slowed bleaching sales, but paler skin became desirable again by the 1980s [1].

sections.h: Ingredients and harms in the category
paras: Skin whiteners have contained hydroquinone, hidden inorganic mercury and corticosteroids. Mercury can cause neurological and kidney problems; hydroquinone has been linked to ochronosis and contact dermatitis; long-term steroid use can thin skin [1]. The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000 [1].
